svg.aria-label: Diagram: what Dedicated Interconnect requires in Google Cloud and what each availability tier costs; the physical prerequisites that your network must meet Google's inside a colocation facility and that you supply your own routing equipment, with single mode fiber at 10, 100 or 400 gigabits and a 10 kilometre optics limit beyond which a lit wavelength or DWDM circuit is needed; the port capacity ladder from one 10-gigabit circuit up to eight 400-gigabit circuits totalling 3200 gigabits, and the fact that the link type cannot be changed after creation so growing capacity means ordering a new connection; the three reliability options of critical production at a 99.99 percent uptime SLA, non-critical production at 99.9 percent, and no SLA; what each tier demands in hardware, with 99.9 percent needing at least two connections in one metro and two VLAN attachments in one region while 99.99 percent needs at least four connections spread across two metros and both edge availability domains of each, plus four attachments split across two regions; the requirement that the multi-region 99.99 percent configuration must use global dynamic routing mode while the single-region variant may use either mode; and the MTU options of 1440, 1460, 1500 or 8896 bytes with Google API client libraries always sending 1440-byte packets regardless
svg.title: Dedicated Interconnect: the SLA is priced in circuits, metros and availability domains
svg.text: The first option in this series where the redundancy is bought in hardware, not configured.
Four posts of tunnels you could create in a console. This one starts with a colocation contract.
What you must have before any of this is possible
Your network must PHYSICALLY MEET Google’s network in a colocation facility, and YOU
MUST PROVIDE YOUR OWN ROUTING EQUIPMENT.
Single mode fiber: 10GBASE-LR (1310 nm), 100GBASE-LR4, or 400GBASE-LR4.
Optics reach 10 km. Further than that from the Google demarcation and you need a lit
wavelength, DWDM, or another managed circuit to close the gap.
The router can sit outside the facility — but then the last stretch is yours to solve.
Port capacity, and the one decision you cannot revisit
1 x 10 Gbps → up to 8 x 10 Gbps = 80 Gbps
1 x 100 Gbps → up to 8 x 100 Gbps = 800 Gbps
1 x 400 Gbps → up to 8 x 400 Gbps = 3200 Gbps
The LINK TYPE CANNOT BE CHANGED LATER. Outgrowing 10-Gbps means ordering a NEW
connection at the higher capacity — not resizing the one you have.
99.9% — non-critical production
• At least TWO connections, in a pair of
facility and edge availability domain
combinations within a SINGLE metro
• At least TWO VLAN attachments, all in
ONE region
• Each attachment on a UNIQUE connection
• At least one Cloud Router in that region
Routing mode: your choice
99.99% — critical production
• At least FOUR connections
• TWO metros: at least two connections in
each, and BOTH edge availability domains
of each metro
• At least FOUR VLAN attachments: two in
one region, two in a DIFFERENT region
• Routing mode: MUST be GLOBAL
• Single-region variant exists: either mode
#84’s setting turns out to be load-bearing for an SLA
For the MULTI-REGION 99.99% configuration, the VPC network MUST use global dynamic
routing mode — because that is what programs learned routes into ALL regions.
For the SINGLE-REGION variant the network may use either mode. So a network-wide setting
introduced as a scope control is, here, a contractual precondition.
Three reliability options on the connection group
CRITICAL PRODUCTION — maximum resiliency. 99.99% uptime SLA.
NON-CRITICAL PRODUCTION — production and development workloads. 99.9% uptime SLA.
NO SLA — available, and honest about what it is.
Two details that bite after the circuits are lit
MTU: a VLAN attachment can be 1440, 1460, 1500 or 8896 bytes. Jumbo frames at 8896 are
supported only on UNENCRYPTED attachments.
But requests to Google API Client Libraries ALWAYS use 1440-byte packets, whatever the
attachment is set to — jumbo frames included. Buying 8896 does not change that traffic.
PRICING: fixed port pricing for outbound data transfer is available, which converts egress
into a fixed monthly invoice rather than a per-gigabyte surprise.
